_work.title: Taysir al-Matalib fi Asrar al-Huruf — Huruf MS (Princeton, 15th c.)
_work.blurb: A 15th-century Arabic manuscript on 'ilm al-huruf (the science of letters), 112 leaves (232 pages), held at Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection). The work is Taysir al-Matalib fi Asrar al-Huruf (Facilitating Goals in the Secrets of Letters) by Kumi Muhammad ibn Muhammad (active 15th century), followed by a second text on the degrees of power of the letters. The manuscript contains extensive tables and charts: magic squares (awfaq) with red-bordered grids, including a spectacular full-page 8×8 wafq thaman (Jupiter magic square), as well as smaller letter-number grids and combinatorial tables of letter values (huruf al-abjad). 'Ilm al-huruf — Islamic lettrism or letter science — holds that the 28 letters of the Arabic alphabet are the structural elements of creation, each carrying elemental, planetary, numerical (abjad), and divine-name correspondences. Practitioners use letter combinations, awfaq, and name-analysis to generate talismans, predict outcomes, and decode the hidden structure of words. The Princeton MS represents the rich 15th-century tradition of learned Islamic letter science in the tradition of al-Buni, Ibn Khaldun, and the Ikhwan al-Safa.
_work.rights: Public Domain — 15th century manuscript. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
_work.creator: Kumi, Muhammad ibn Muhammad (active 15th century)

entries.title: Wafq Thaman — Full-Page 8×8 Arabic Magic Square (Jupiter Square) — Huruf MS (p. 57)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, red-ink borders
entries.rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
entries.summary: A spectacular full-page 8×8 magic square (wafq thaman) from a 15th-century Princeton manuscript on 'ilm al-huruf (the science of letters). The grid is drawn with red-ink borders framing all cells; each of the 64 cells contains an Arabic numeral and a letter designation, with corner labels and subsidiary text indicating the square's planetary and divine-name associations. In Islamic letter science, the 8×8 magic square is associated with Jupiter (Mushtari) and its divine name; its cells sum to 260 in each row, column, and diagonal (the standard 8×8 = 8 × 33 = 260 structure). The grid occupies the full page below the Arabic text column, demonstrating that the wafq here is not an illustration but an operative element — a talisman to be copied, carried, or inscribed on metal or cloth. The red-ink border system serves double duty: structurally organizing the grid and visually marking it as sacred space, in the same tradition as al-Buni's Shams al-Ma'arif where red ink designates the diagrammatic and the divine.

entries.title: Wafq Letter-Number Grid — Huruf MS (p. 59)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, red-ink borders
entries.rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
entries.summary: A wafq (magic square) from a 15th-century Princeton huruf MS, bordered in red ink with Arabic numerals and letter designations in each cell. This grid, immediately following the 8×8 Jupiter square (p. 57), shows a different configuration — smaller grid, different letter-number assignments — indicating sequential treatment of multiple awfaq types within the same section of the text. In 'ilm al-huruf, each wafq type encodes a specific divine name, element (fire/water/air/earth), humor (hot/cold/wet/dry), planetary assignment, and set of uses (healing, love, protection, coercion). The red-bordered grid page functions simultaneously as a textual element (part of the exposition) and as a replicable talisman template — the practitioner is expected to copy it exactly onto a suitable medium. The red ink tradition links this Princeton MS directly to the North African Buniyan tradition of the Shams al-Ma'arif.

entries.title: Alif Chapter Wafq Grid — Huruf MS (p. 18)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, red-ink borders
entries.rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
entries.summary: A red-bordered wafq grid from the opening chapter (Fasl al-Awwal fi Harf al-Alif — First Chapter on the Letter Alif) of the Taysir al-Matalib fi Asrar al-Huruf. The grid appears in the upper right of the page alongside explanatory text in Arabic, showing the numeric and letter assignments specific to the letter alif in the system of 'ilm al-huruf. In the huruf tradition, each of the 28 Arabic letters has a corresponding wafq (magic square), abjad value, elemental and planetary assignment, and set of divine names. The Alif — the first letter, associated with divine unity (tawhid) — receives the first and most fundamental wafq treatment. The red-ink ruled border follows the standard format seen throughout this MS and connects it to the wider tradition of Buniyan lettrism where red demarcates the operative/diagrammatic elements from commentary text.

entries.title: Wafq with Overlapping Circles — 4×4 Grid (Huruf MS, p. 21)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, red-ink borders and circles
entries.rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
entries.summary: A visually striking full-page wafq grid from the Taysir al-Matalib (Princeton), labeled 'Surat Wad'uhu' (Image/Form of its Placement). The 4×4 magic square is drawn with an overlay of red-ink circular arcs — overlapping circles connecting adjacent cells in a floral interlace pattern — so that the visual result reads simultaneously as a grid and as a rosette or ring-chain geometric figure. Each cell contains an Arabic divine name or letter value. In 'ilm al-huruf, the wafq serves not only as a calculated numeric/alphabetic arrangement but as a visual talisman whose geometric form carries intrinsic power; the circle-overlay amplifies this visual-talismanic quality, transforming the abstract grid into an ornamental form suitable for inscription on talisman media. The use of overlapping-circle geometry in Islamic talismanic art is widespread — it appears in architectural tilework, in seal designs, and in manuscript borders — and this page fuses the mathematical with the ornamental in a single operative image.

entries.title: Wafq Numeric 4×4 Grid — Huruf MS (p. 24)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, red-ink borders
entries.rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
entries.summary: A red-bordered 4×4 numeric magic square from the Taysir al-Matalib (Princeton), positioned at the top of a text page with a chapter heading reading 'Al-Dhikr al-Qa'im ma'...' (The Standing/Remaining Dhikr with...). The cells contain Arabic numerals representing a 4×4 magic square — a wafq associated with Jupiter (16-cell Jupiter squares, summing to 34 in each row/column) or another planetary/elemental figure. Following the Alif-chapter wafq (p. 18) and the circle-wafq (p. 21), this page shows the third consecutive wafq in the opening section, establishing the density of the huruf practice in this MS: each chapter or sub-chapter of letter-science begins with or includes its operative wafq.

entries.title: Large Numeric Wafq with Divine Names Column — Huruf MS (p. 41)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, red-ink borders
entries.rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
entries.summary: A substantial wafq diagram from the Taysir al-Matalib (Princeton) occupying the upper half of the page. The grid has multiple rows and a side column containing divine names of God (asma' Allah) — including al-Alim, al-Jabir (the Wise, the Compeller) — alongside the numeric entries in the main grid cells. The combination of a numeric magic square with a list of divine names identifies this as a named-attribute wafq: a magic square whose construction encodes specific divine attributes, used to draw down the corresponding divine quality for the practitioner's purpose. The labeled divine names in red ink beside the grid serve both as a key (identifying which wafq this is) and as an operative element (the names are part of the talisman's power). This page comes approximately midway through the MS, in the middle letters of the Arabic alphabet, showing that major wafq diagrams appear throughout all 232 pages of this letter-science compendium.

entries.title: Full-Page Large Wafq Grid — Huruf MS (p. 69)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, red-ink borders
entries.rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
entries.summary: The most visually dominant single-page wafq in the Taysir al-Matalib (Princeton) — a large, full-page magic square occupying almost the entire leaf, with red-ink ruled borders and a heading in red Arabic text reading 'wa-hiya surat al-wafq' (This is the image/form of the wafq). The grid is substantially larger than the 8×8 Jupiter square (p. 57) and the other wafqs in this MS; each cell contains a red Arabic numeral. The heading explicitly names this as 'the image of the wafq' — a formulation used in huruf texts when the diagram is being presented as a talisman template for reproduction, not just an illustration. The large physical size means the MS was meant to be opened to this page and the wafq copied in full on metal, cloth, or paper for operative use. The preponderance of red ink — both in the ruling and in the numerals — marks this as a particularly significant talisman in the sequence.

entries.title: Hexagram Khatim Talisman Circle — Huruf MS (p. 137)
entries.rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
entries.summary: A circular khatim (talisman seal) diagram from the Taysir al-Matalib (Princeton) featuring a large hexagram (six-pointed star, known in Islamic magic as Khatim Sulayman — the Seal of Solomon or Star of David) inscribed within a circle. Arabic numerals fill the triangular cells of the star and the surrounding regions; the outer ring and angular points carry additional letter-number notations. The text above identifies the context (divine name or purpose). The Seal of Solomon / hexagram is one of the most widely used Islamic talisman forms, appearing in Arabic, Persian, and Hebrew magical traditions as a binding seal against malevolent spirits and as a charm for protection, love, and victory. In 'ilm al-huruf tradition, the hexagram khatim is drawn with specific abjad values at specific points to encode a divine name or Quranic verse; each numeral placement is determined by the letter-science of the huruf practitioner. This Princeton example comes late in the MS (p. 137 of 232), in a section apparently focused on khatim/seal designs rather than magic squares.
